chunks: "There are really a few loops stacked on top of each other, running at different speeds. The fastest and most basic one is on the chip itself.
Thermal sensors, usually a diode whose voltage changes with temperature, feed a small controller.
When the junction gets close to its limit, say within ten degrees, it starts throttling: it drops the clock or the voltage and frequency through DVFS, or caps power.
That's often a simple threshold with hysteresis, so it doesn't flap on and off, or a stepped governor that walks through frequency states. The next loop is at the system level.
A fan controller reads temperature and sets fan PWM, usually along a temperature-to-speed curve or a PID, because a fan can cool the chip without costing performance.
The OS or firmware can also manage things with workload migration or by parking cores, and phones with no fan lean entirely on throttling and skin-temperature limits.
Last is the safety net: if everything else fails, a hardware trip shuts the part down at a fixed temperature, independent of software.
The thing to keep in mind is that the thermal plant is slow, with a time constant of seconds, so the loops are cautious.
Too aggressive and you oscillate; too gentle and you overshoot the limit."
